item.title: Businesses Report Cautious Economic Outlook – Business Outlook Survey in October
item.description:
Businesses reported cautious expectations for their economic performance in October. Intensified attacks on energy, production, storage and logistics infrastructure, the resumption of power cuts, rising fuel prices, restricted exports due to port blockades, and a shortage of skilled labor dampened companies’ economic activity. Sustained consumer demand, the bumper harvest, an ample supply of goods, and the establishment of new logistics routes remained growth drivers. This is evidenced by the business activity expectations index (BAEI), which the NBU calculates every month, apart from a forced break in March–May 2022. The business activity expectations index (BAEI) was 47.1 in October, down from 48.2 in September 2026 and 50.3 in October 2025.

Industrial companies took a restrained view of their economic performance, citing the destruction of production facilities, energy shortages, and constrained exports caused by port blockades, the sectoral index being 48.0 in October, compared to 51.0 in September and 48.8 in October 2025. In contrast to the previous month, respondents expected a drop in the number of new orders for products, including export orders, and in stocks of raw materials and supplies. At the same time, industrial companies continued to expect an increase in their manufactured goods volumes, albeit at a slower pace. Respondents reported dimmer expectations about the amount of unfinished products (unfulfilled orders) and finished goods stocks.

On the back of the ongoing suspension of state funding for road and infrastructure reconstruction, a shortage of skilled labor and seasonal factors, construction companies reported the most cautious economic outlook among all sectors, the sectoral index being 38.5 in October, compared to 48.8 in September and 53.3 in October 2025. Following seven months of optimism, respondents expected a noticeable drop in construction volumes, the number of new orders, and in purchases of raw materials and supplies. Construction companies said they intended to purchase fewer contractor services amid sustained growth in the cost of these services and dimmer expectations about contractors’ availability.

Trading companies have reported a restrained economic outlook for three months running, driven by ongoing damage to warehousing facilities and rising transport and storage costs, the sectoral index being 46.8 in October, compared to 45.9 in September and 54.3 in October 2025. Respondents expected a further decrease in their trade turnover and in purchases of goods for sale, albeit at a slightly slower pace. Companies continued to expect a drop in their stocks of goods for sale and said they intended to cut their trading margins further.

Due to the ongoing destruction of transport and warehousing facilities, higher fuel prices, and a shortage of skilled labor, services companies continued to report restrained expectations for their economic performance, the sectoral index being 47.4 in October, compared to 47.3 in September and 48.7 in October 2025. In contrast to the previous month, companies expected a decline in the amount of services provided. Furthermore, respondents expected a decrease in the number of new orders for services and in the amount of services that are being provided.

Respondents across most of the surveyed sectors continued to expect rapid growth in purchase prices / raw material and supplies prices, declaring intentions to raise their selling prices at a fast pace. Only services companies expected weaker growth in purchase prices and said they intended to raise their selling prices more slowly.

Labor market conditions were unstable. In contrast to the previous month, companies across all sectors said they intended to reduce their workforces, with the construction sector declaring the strongest intentions.

Background

This survey was carried out from 5 October through 22 October 2026. A total of 587 companies were polled. Of the companies polled, 41.9% are industrial companies, 26.9% services companies, 25.0% trading companies, and 6.1% construction companies; 31.2% of the respondents are large companies, 28.3% medium companies, and 40.5% small companies. Of the surveyed companies, 34.8% are both exporters and importers, 8.5% are exporters only, 17.5% are importers only, and 39.2% are neither exporters nor importers.

The findings presented reflect only the opinions of the respondents (top managers of companies), and should not be considered as NBU assessments.

The monthly business activity expectations index (BAEI) is a tool for conducting the latest assessments and detecting trends in economic development. It is calculated on the basis of surveys of Ukrainian real sector companies regarding changes in their performance compared to the previous month.

Monthly business activity expectations indices are calculated on the basis of respondents’ replies. These indices are as follows: sectoral indices (for each sector of the economy) and a composite index (describes the country’s economic performance over a month). A value of 50 corresponds to the neutral level. Index values above the neutral level indicate positive expectations.

Read more about the October 2026 survey in the Monthly Surveys of Companies Subsection of the Publications Section on the NBU’s official website.

The NBU posts monthly survey results in the open data format.

The results of the next (November 2026) survey will be published on the first business day of December 2026.

item.title: NBU Updates Approaches to Banks’ Access to Transactions with NBU Certificates of Deposit
item.description:
The National Bank of Ukraine has updated its approaches to granting banks access to transactions with NBU certificates of deposit (hereinafter referred to as “NBU CDs”) if the banks’ ownership structures include qualifying holders subject to sanctions or qualifying holders that have been ordered to divest their qualifying holdings in the bank.

Transactions to place NBU CDs in tenders conducted by the NBU and transactions to purchase NBU CDs from other banks in the interbank market are prohibited for:

  1. Banks with sanctioned qualifying holders.

Such banks’ access to all or some transactions with NBU CDs can be restored on the basis of a relevant decision by the Committee on Banking Regulation and Supervision and Oversight of Payment Infrastructures of the National Bank of Ukraine (hereinafter referred to as the “Supervision Committee”). The decision is adopted taking into account the banks’ impact on the sustainability of the banking system.

  1. Banks with sanctioned qualifying holders with respect to which the NBU has decided to temporarily suspend their voting rights and appoint a trustee to whom the voting rights associated with the relevant shares have been transferred.

Access to all or some transactions with NBU CDs can be restored for such banks based on a relevant decision by the Supervision Committee, which is adopted taking into account the impact on the sustainability of the banking system and/or the need to protect the interests of the bank’s creditors and depositors.

  1. Banks against which the NBU has imposed an enforcement measure in the form of a requirement to divest the bank’s shares.

Such banks may regain access to all or some transactions with NBU CDs after complying with the requirement to divest the bank’s shares held by the qualifying holder and to establish a new ownership structure approved by the NBU.

The relevant amendments were approved by NBU Board Resolution No. 124 On Amendments to NBU Board Resolution No. 22 dated 24 February 2022 dated 28 October 2026, which takes effect on 1 December 2026.

For reference

Banks with sanctioned qualifying holders are banks that have in their ownership structure qualifying holders or ultimate beneficial owners who are citizens of a state waging armed aggression against Ukraine, as defined in Article 1 of the Law of Ukraine  On Defense of Ukraine, or legal persons registered in such a state. This also applies if sanctions have been imposed against the bank and/or ultimate beneficial owners of the bank and/or qualifying holders in the bank by Ukraine, foreign states (except states waging armed aggression against Ukraine), interstate associations, or international organizations.

item.title: Speech by NBU Governor Andriy Pyshnyy at Press Briefing on Monetary Policy Decisions
item.description:
Dear colleagues,

The Board of the National Bank of Ukraine has decided to raise the key policy rate to 16.5% in view of a significant increase in price pressures and a deterioration in inflation expectations.

This decision will support the attractiveness of hryvnia assets and the sustainability of the FX market, allowing to keep inflation expectations and price dynamics in check.

The NBU stands ready to respond flexibly to further changes in the balance of risks, taking into account both the persistence of price pressures and potential effects of weaker economic activity.

Price pressures have increased markedly due to the consequences of russia’s attacks on business and logistics as well as due to the surge in fuel prices

In recent months, inflation has continued to rise, noticeably exceeding the NBU’s previous forecast. In September, headline inflation accelerated to 10.0% yoy and core inflation increased to 8.8% yoy. These trends continued in October, according to the NBU’s estimates.

Inflation dynamics were driven primarily by direct and second-round effects from the surge in fuel prices caused by the war in the Middle East, as well as the intensification of russia’s attacks on warehousing and logistical infrastructure of Ukraine.

In such conditions, inflation expectations of households remained volatile and high, while those of the banks and analysts worsened significantly.

Inflation will return to a decline in 2027 as effects of higher fuel prices wane and thanks to the NBU's monetary policy measures

The inflation forecast for 2026 has been revised upward, to 12.5%. The NBU estimates that consequences of aerial attacks alone will add around 0.7 pp to annual inflation. Other important factors affecting the price dynamics will include effects of higher fuel prices and an expansion of fiscal stimulus.

Inflation will slow to 7.3% yoy in 2027. This should be facilitated by the expected decrease in global prices for crude oil as well as by monetary policy measures. The NBU will continue to support the attractiveness of hryvnia assets and the sustainability of the FX market, which will rein in price pressures. Inflation will also be restrained by the likely cooling of domestic demand and the labor market in the coming months due to consequences of russia’s attacks.

As before, inflation is expected to return to the 5% target in 2028. A gradual easing of the pressure on businesses’ production costs and an increase in domestic supply of goods and services are important preconditions for this.

russia’s attacks have led to a sharp fall in business activity, and losses in  economic potential will constrain recovery

According to the NBU’s estimates, real GDP decreased by 0.5% yoy in Q3. Such dynamics were driven primarily by the consequences of the sea port blockade and russia’s attacks on production facilities and logistics. Metallurgical and ore mining enterprises suffered the greatest losses. At the same time, performance also deteriorated in other industrial sectors, trade, and agriculture.

As a result, the NBU revised the real GDP forecast for 2026 downward, to (-0.4%). Consequences of intensified aerial attacks had the biggest impact on the worsening of the forecast, with their negative contribution to GDP being estimated at 1.9 pp.

Considering the consequences of the inflicted damage, the NBU projects economic growth to recover slowly in 2027–2028. A revival of economic activity will be supported, among other things, by public and private investment in the defense industry, localization of weapon production financed by Ukraine Support Loan, and projects to reconstruct critical infrastructure. If the NBU’s technical assumption about the improvement in logistics in mid-2027 materializes, real GDP may grow by 0.4% next year. In 2028, economic growth will speed up to 2.2% as security risks subside.

External assistance remains crucial for supporting macrofinancial stability

Volumes of international financial assistance in Q3 were smaller than expected, primarily due to Ukraine delaying the implementation of reforms. That said, in October, the parliament adopted a number of laws to unblock the financing form the EU and the IMF. The pace of fulfilling commitments under support programs is expected to be caught up further, which will lower the uncertainty about sources of budget financing.

The NBU’s forecast envisages Ukraine to receive around USD 50 billion of direct budget support and more than USD 32 billion under the defense component of Ukraine Support Loan in 2026. USD 52 billion and USD 37 billion, respectively, are assumed to be received in 2027. Such volumes of assistance would allow financing large budget needs and maintaining international reserves at a comfortable level (more than USD 62 billion in 2026–2027).

The course of the full-scale war remains the key risk to inflation dynamics and economic development; however, longer-lasting hostilities in the Middle East could also have a significant impact

The war is continuing. The intensification of russia’s targeted attacks on production facilities and infrastructure in recent months has significantly heightened inflation risks associated, in particular, with rising production costs and a decline in the supply of goods and services.

The following war-related risks are also relevant:

  • the emergence of additional budgetary needs to support defense capabilities and reconstruction, with a corresponding expansion of domestic demand, including demand for imports
  • elevated wage pressures due to a deepening labor shortage and negative migration trends.

Risks of disruptions to the timing and/or changes to the volumes of international financing persist. However, these risks have decreased thanks to Ukraine’s fulfillment of some of its obligations under support programs and preliminary signals from partners regarding financing for the next year.

The risks associated with the war in the Middle East, primarily those related to higher oil prices, are also significant. High energy prices are hampering economic growth and increasing price pressures in Ukraine, while simultaneously fueling russian aggression.

At the same time, a further deterioration in the security situation could lead to a noticeable cooling in domestic demand, which would have a disinflationary effect. In addition, difficulties in exporting due to port blockades may contribute to a short-term decline in purchase prices for certain food products.

That said, there remains the potential for a more favorable turn of events linked to the achievement of significant progress in securing a just and lasting peace for Ukraine.

To retain the attractiveness of hryvnia assets, maintain FX market sustainability, keep expectations under control, and to gradually bring inflation back to its 5% target over the policy horizon, the NBU Board decided to raise the key policy rate by 0.5 pp, to 16.5%

Previous steps to tighten interest rate policy have bolstered the appeal of hryvnia assets. As is usually the case, small banks were the first to respond to the hike in the key policy rate; however, over the past month, large financial institutions with a significant market share have also begun to adjust their interest rates on hryvnia deposits.

As a result, robust demand for hryvnia savings persisted. Hryvnia retail deposits and investments in hryvnia domestic government debt securities continued to grow.

The October hike in the key policy rate will strengthen the transmission of previous decisions, which will help maintain the attractiveness of hryvnia assets.

This decision will also help contain pressures on the FX market, which have intensified due to a decline in exports and worsening expectations amid escalating russian attacks on businesses and civilians.

Tightening monetary policy to curb inflation aligns with the NBU’s goal of supporting the economy

Price stability is an essential prerequisite for restoring stable economic growth and sustainable lending development. A moderate increase in the key policy rate is a well-considered decision that helps maintain a balance between keeping inflation in check and supporting the economy.

Despite the NBU’s tightening its interest rate policy, lending growth remained robust. In September 2026, growth in net hryvnia corporate loans exceeded 32% yoy, while net retail loans grew by over 38% yoy.

The NBU continues to place significant emphasis on further supporting lending to sectors that are priorities for defense and economic resiliense. In recent months, the NBU has adopted four packages of regulatory changes aimed, among other things, at supporting companies in the defense, energy, agriculture and trade sectors.

The NBU stands ready to respond flexibly to further changes in the balance of risks, taking into account both the persistence of price pressures and potential effects of weaker economic activity.

The NBU forecast envisages maintaining the key policy rate at the current level until Q2 2027. At the same time, the NBU will respond flexibly to actual developments, taking into account the impact of russian attacks on inflation dynamics and economic activity.

Thank you for your attention!

Glory to Ukraine!

item.title: NBU Raises Key Policy Rate to 16.5%
item.description:
The Board of the National Bank of Ukraine has decided to raise the key policy rate to 16.5% in view of a significant increase in price pressures and a deterioration in inflation expectations. This decision will support the attractiveness of hryvnia assets and the sustainability of the FX market, allowing to keep inflation expectations and price dynamics in check. The NBU stands ready to respond flexibly to further changes in the balance of risks, taking into account both the persistence of price pressures and potential effects of weaker economic activity.

Price pressures have increased markedly due to the consequences of russia’s attacks on business and logistics as well as due to the surge in fuel prices

In recent months, inflation has continued to rise, noticeably exceeding the NBU’s previous forecast (Inflation Report, July 2026). In September, headline inflation accelerated to 10.0% yoy and core inflation increased to 8.8% yoy. These trends continued in October, according to the NBU’s estimates. Inflation dynamics were driven primarily by direct and second-round effects from the surge in fuel prices caused by the war in the Middle East, as well as the intensification of russia’s attacks on warehousing and logistical infrastructure of Ukraine. In such conditions, inflation expectations of households remained volatile and high, while those of the banks and analysts worsened significantly.

Inflation will return to a decline in 2027 as effects of higher fuel prices wane and thanks to the NBU's monetary policy measures

The inflation forecast for 2026 has been revised upward, to 12.5%. The NBU estimates that consequences of aerial attacks alone will add around 0.7 pp to annual inflation. Other important factors affecting the price dynamics will include effects of higher fuel prices and an expansion of fiscal stimulus.

Inflation will slow to 7.3% yoy in 2027. This should be facilitated by the expected decrease in global prices for crude oil as well as by monetary policy measures. The NBU will continue to support the attractiveness of hryvnia assets and the sustainability of the FX market, which will rein in price pressures. Inflation will also be restrained by the likely cooling of domestic demand and the labor market in the coming months due to consequences of russia’s attacks.

As before, inflation is expected to return to the 5% target in 2028. A gradual easing of the pressure on businesses’ production costs and an increase in domestic supply of goods and services are important preconditions for this.

russia’s attacks have led to a sharp fall in business activity, and losses in  economic potential will constrain recovery

According to the NBU’s estimates, real GDP decreased by 0.5% yoy in Q3. Such dynamics were driven primarily by the consequences of the sea port blockade and russia’s attacks on production facilities and logistics. Metallurgical and ore mining enterprises suffered the greatest losses. At the same time, performance also deteriorated in other industrial sectors, trade, and agriculture. As a result, the NBU revised the real GDP forecast for 2026 downward, to (-0.4%). Consequences of intensified aerial attacks had the biggest impact on the worsening of the forecast, with their negative contribution to GDP being estimated at 1.9 pp.

Considering the consequences of the inflicted damage, the NBU projects economic growth to recover slowly in 2027–2028. A revival of economic activity will be supported, among other things, by public and private investment in the defense industry, localization of weapon production financed by Ukraine Support Loan, and projects to reconstruct critical infrastructure. If the NBU’s technical assumption about the improvement in logistics in mid-2027 materializes, real GDP may grow by 0.4% next year. In 2028, economic growth will speed up to 2.2% as security risks subside.

External assistance remains crucial for supporting macrofinancial stability

Volumes of international financial assistance in Q3 were smaller than expected, primarily due to Ukraine delaying the implementation of reforms. That said, in October, the parliament adopted a number of laws to unblock the financing form the EU and the IMF. The pace of fulfilling commitments under support programs is expected to be caught up further, which will lower the uncertainty about sources of budget financing.

The NBU’s forecast envisages Ukraine to receive around USD 50 billion of direct budget support and more than USD 32 billion under the defense component of Ukraine Support Loan in 2026. USD 52 billion and USD 37 billion, respectively, are assumed to be received in 2027. Such volumes of assistance would allow financing large budget needs and maintaining international reserves at a comfortable level (more than USD 62 billion in 2026–2027).

The course of the full-scale war remains the key risk to inflation dynamics and economic development; however, longer-lasting hostilities in the Middle East could also have a significant impact

The war is continuing. The intensification of russia’s targeted attacks on production facilities and infrastructure in recent months has significantly heightened inflation risks associated, in particular, with rising production costs and a decline in the supply of goods and services.

The following war-related risks are also relevant:

  • the emergence of additional budgetary needs to support defense capabilities and reconstruction, with a corresponding expansion of domestic demand, including demand for imports
  • elevated wage pressures due to a deepening labor shortage and negative migration trends.

Risks of disruptions to the timing and/or changes to the volumes of international financing persist. However, these risks have decreased thanks to Ukraine’s fulfillment of some of its obligations under support programs and preliminary signals from partners regarding financing for the next year.

The risks associated with the war in the Middle East, primarily those related to higher oil prices, are also significant. High energy prices are hampering economic growth and increasing price pressures in Ukraine, while simultaneously fueling russian aggression.

At the same time, a further deterioration in the security situation could lead to a noticeable cooling in domestic demand, which would have a disinflationary effect. In addition, difficulties in exporting due to port blockades may contribute to a short-term decline in purchase prices for certain food products.

That said, there remains the potential for a more favorable turn of events linked to the achievement of significant progress in securing a just and lasting peace for Ukraine.

To retain the attractiveness of hryvnia assets, maintain FX market sustainability, keep expectations under control, and to gradually bring inflation back to its 5% target over the policy horizon, the NBU Board decided to raise the key policy rate by 0.5 pp, to 16.5%

Previous steps to tighten interest rate policy have bolstered the appeal of hryvnia assets. As is usually the case, small banks were the first to respond to the hike in the key policy rate; however, over the past month, large financial institutions with a significant market share have also begun to adjust their interest rates on hryvnia deposits. As a result, robust demand for hryvnia savings persisted. Hryvnia retail deposits and investments in hryvnia domestic government debt securities continued to grow.

The October hike in the key policy rate will strengthen the transmission of previous decisions, which will help maintain the attractiveness of hryvnia assets. This decision will also help contain pressures on the FX market, which have intensified due to a decline in exports and worsening expectations amid escalating russian attacks on businesses and civilians.

Tightening monetary policy to curb inflation aligns with the NBU’s goal of supporting the economy

Price stability is an essential prerequisite for restoring stable economic growth and sustainable lending development. A moderate increase in the key policy rate is a well-considered decision that helps maintain a balance between keeping inflation in check and supporting the economy.

Despite the NBU’s tightening its interest rate policy, lending growth remained robust. In September 2026, growth in net hryvnia corporate loans exceeded 32% yoy, while net retail loans grew by over 38% yoy.

The NBU continues to place significant emphasis on further supporting lending to sectors that are priorities for defense and economic resiliense. In recent months, the NBU has adopted four packages of regulatory changes aimed, among other things, at supporting companies in the defense, energy, agriculture and trade sectors.

The NBU stands ready to respond flexibly to further changes in the balance of risks, taking into account both the persistence of price pressures and potential effects of weaker economic activity.

The NBU forecast envisages maintaining the key policy rate at the current level until Q2 2027. At the same time, the NBU will respond flexibly to actual developments, taking into account the impact of russian attacks on inflation dynamics and economic activity.

The detailed October macroeconomic forecast will be published in the Inflation Report on 5 November 2026.

The decision to raise the key policy rate, to 16,5% per annum, was approved by NBU Board Decision on the key policy rate No. 369, dated 29 October 2026, which will come into effect on 30 October 2026.

A summary of the discussion by Monetary Policy Committee members that preceded the approval of this decision will be published on 9 November 2026.

The next monetary policy meeting of the NBU Board will be held on 17 December 2026, according to the confirmed and published schedule.

item.title: Press Briefing on Monetary Policy Decisions
Banks Increase Volumes of Client Deposits and Raise Rates on Them – Bank Funding Survey
item.description:
The volume of client deposits at the banks have increased, primarily from households, while interest rates on these deposits have risen largely due to higher rates on corporate deposits. This is according to the results of the Bank Funding Survey.

Key findings of the survey for Q3 2026:

  • The amount of bank liabilities as a whole have increased – mainly due to the growth in household deposits.
  • Volumes of wholesale funding have been on the rise since mid-2025, primarily on account of loans from international financial institutions and development banks.
  • Going forward, the banks expect an increase in retail and corporate deposits, as well as in wholesale funding.
  • The average cost of borrowing has risen due to higher interest rates on corporate deposits and, to some extent, on retail ones, although the cost of wholesale funding has remained virtually unchanged.
  • The banks forecast an increase in the cost of funding and a rise in interest rates on business and household deposits, as well as in the cost of wholesale funding.
  • The share of FX liabilities has grown slightly, but it is expected to remain unchanged further on.
  • The maturity of funding has increased, and financial institutions expect it to continue to rise.
  • The majority of the banks reported an increase in total capital over the past 12 months and said they expect this uptrend to last.
  • The banks have once again cited profitability as a key driver of capital growth.
  • For the first time since Q1 2025, the respondents expect a rise in the cost of capital.
For reference

The current bank funding survey was carried out from 16 September through 7 October 2026 among bank liability managers. The responses were provided by 25 financial institutions, which together held 95% of the banking system’s total assets. The results of the survey reflect the opinions of respondents and are not estimates or forecasts of the NBU. The survey on expectations for Q1 2027 will be published in January 2027.

item.title: Banks Expect Further Growth in Business and Household Loan Portfolios – Bank Lending Survey
item.description:
The banks expect business and household loan portfolios to grow over the next 12 months, while the balance of responses regarding changes in corporate loan volumes is at its lowest level since Q2 2023. This is according to the results of the Bank Lending Survey.

Key findings of the survey for Q3:

  • Demand for business loans has increased overall, but for the first time since the start of 2023, there has been no increase in demand from SMEs or for hryvnia-denominated loans.
  • The banks expect a rise in the demand for all types of business loans, and especially for loans to large enterprises and short-term and hryvnia loans.
  • Households’ demand for loans has increased slightly, and the banks expect demand for consumer loans to rise; however, for the first time since late 2024, they anticipate a decline in demand for mortgages.
  • The debt burden of large enterprises remained moderate, while that of SMEs and households remained low.
  • The respondents expect the quality of loans to businesses and households to deteriorate, particularly with regard to the household loan portfolio – for the fifth consecutive quarter.
  • Lending standards for the corporate sector have tightened, and the banks plan to further tighten standards, particularly for large enterprises.
  • The approval rate for corporate loan applications has declined for the first time since mid-2024. The banks noted higher interest rates and stricter collateral requirements when approving applications.
  • The banks have loosened lending standards for mortgages and consumer loans and expect them to ease further.
  • The approval rate for retail loan applications has increased, especially for mortgages.
  • The banks reported an increase in all types of risks and expect them to rise further – particularly credit risk and FX risk.
For reference

The Bank Lending Survey was held among credit managers of the banks between 16 September and 7 October 2026. Responses were provided by 25 financial institutions, which accounted for 95% of the banking system’s assets. The survey’s results reflect the views of respondents and are not assessments or forecasts by the NBU. The survey of expectations for Q1 2027 will be published in January 2027.

item.title: Speech by Andriy Pyshnyy at IMF’s Regional Economic Outlook for Central, Eastern, and Southeastern Europe
item.description:
Event held on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank Group Annual Meetings in Bangkok.

Dear colleagues,

Thank you for the presentation and the opportunity to join the discussion.

We share the IMF’s key findings. Decisive policies and structural reforms are critically important for sustainable economic growth in Central, Eastern, and Southeastern Europe.

Geopolitical uncertainty and major shocks have become our reality.

It is precisely under these circumstances that we must not only ensure macroeconomic stability but also create the conditions for long-term growth.

In this context, I would like to focus on three points.

First. Energy resilience is a fundamental prerequisite for macroeconomic stability.

The new energy shock caused by the war in the Middle East has once again reminded us of our vulnerability.

High energy prices affect all sectors. They increase inflationary pressures, constrain economic growth, and undermine business competitiveness and external trade balances.

Recent years have taught us that diversifying energy supplies, developing distributed generation, and improving energy efficiency are critical necessities.

And sometimes, to ensure Europe’s energy resilience, energy supply in certain locations needs to be reduced. After all, it is this supply that ultimately generates the resources used to undermine that resilience.

Ukraine’s experience is instructive. For the fifth consecutive year, we have been operating amid systematic russian attacks on our energy infrastructure.

The development of distributed generation, the expansion of cross-border energy interconnections, and business investment in autonomous energy supply have laid the foundation for energy resilience.

Coupled with strengthening the financial system’s ability to operate uninterruptedly under such shocks, these efforts have laid the groundwork for macroeconomic stability.

Second. Monetary policy must remain consistent even amid persistent supply shocks.

The effects of such shocks may last much longer than initially expected.

Higher energy prices and disruptions to production chains and logistics eventually translate into higher production costs and mounting underlying inflationary pressures.

The key task for central banks is to prevent temporary shocks from causing a persistent unanchoring of inflation expectations.

This requires flexibility in the choice of instruments and unwavering commitment to objectives.

With uncertainty running high, central bank independence, policy consistency, and policy credibility are more important than ever.

At the same time, rising fiscal needs increase the importance of a coordinated macroeconomic policy mix. Fiscal policy must not create additional obstacles to ensuring price stability.

Third. Sustainable economic growth requires a shift from adapting to shocks to systematically increasing productivity.

The IMF rightly emphasizes that traditional drivers of growth in our region are gradually weakening.

Demographic challenges, labor shortages, and intensifying competition in external markets are all constraining further economic convergence with more advanced economies.

Private investment, innovation, digitalization, automation, and productivity gains are becoming increasingly important.

European integration is an important catalyst for these processes. For EU candidate countries, it provides additional incentives for structural reforms and institutional development.

Ukraine’s recovery also opens up new opportunities for the entire region through the development of cross-border infrastructure, industrial cooperation, and integration into European value-added chains.

We need to harness this potential to drive structural transformation and enhance the competitiveness of our economies.

Reforms must be implemented proactively, rather than waiting for structural problems to become obstacles to economic growth.

To conclude.

The challenges facing our region’s economies increasingly transcend national borders.

Addressing them therefore requires closer coordination and international partnerships.

Europe cannot be truly resilient if each country is forced to tackle shared challenges on its own. Europe’s strength lies not only in the resilience of individual states but also in their ability to act together. This is what transforms national resilience into shared European strength.

Thank you.

item.title: NBU Hosts Third International Scientific Conference “Money & Banking: Monetary Reforms”
item.description:
The 3rd International Scientific Conference “Money & Banking: Monetary Reforms” was held online by the NBU on 8–9 October 2026.

For three consecutive years, the conference has brought together scholars and researchers to explore lesser-known chapters in monetary history and discuss trends and challenges in contemporary banknote and coin design.

It served as a platform for experience exchange among foreign and Ukrainian experts in the history of money circulation, economic history, numismatics, banking history, art history, linguistics, and archaeology.

In total, around 50 researchers from Ukraine and across Europe participated in the event, including representatives from the European Central Bank and the central banks of Poland, Turkey, and Lithuania.

“The history of money is the history of states, institutions, and societies,” noted Oleksii Shaban, Deputy Governor of the NBU, in his opening remarks. “By studying past monetary reforms, we gain a deeper understanding of how trust in currency and state institutions was forged, which decisions stood the test of time, and how the role of money in society evolved. Consequently, this gives us a clearer vision and understanding of the future.”

The event agenda featured two thematic sessions:

  • Monetary Reforms
  • Numismatics and the History of Monetary Circulation.

On the first day, participants heard from representatives of the European Central Bank and the central banks of the above European countries. The international speakers highlighted the vital role of effective public communications during monetary reforms, banknote and coin redesigns, and the selection of themes for commemorative coin series.

The afternoon featured break-out sessions where Ukrainian researchers presented in-depth findings on the historical significance of monetary reforms at various stages of Ukraine’s and world history.

The second day focused on a broad range of topics in numismatics and monetary circulation history. Scholars showcased research covering ancient and medieval coin minting, including studies on Thracian coins in Tyras and Olbia, Roman denarii and antoniniani, monetary imitations of Jani Beg, and Podolia half-groschen.

During the break-out sessions, participants engaged in lively discussions on money circulation and regional monetary systems (from the 18th to the early 20th centuries), focusing on coin finds in Budzhak and Crimea, as well as the impact of russian and Austro-Hungarian imperial monetary policies on Ukraine.

Ukrainian researchers shared major, previously unpublished contributions to the study of paper money, securities, notaphily, and quasimoney – including competition design sketches for UPR banknotes, land bank and oil & gas company securities, non-governmental and bonus stamps, and wartime monetary policy.

Attention was also drawn to modern numismatics and commemorative coins in Ukraine and worldwide, covering the evolution of memorial narratives on NBU coins, commemorative coin finishes and types, the shah concept, and minting innovations.

Special recognition goes to presentations that tackled important issues regarding the assessment of lost numismatic artifacts, as well as the anthropological and philosophical dimensions of monetary studies.

Over the two days, the live stream of the conference drew over 9,000 views and brought together nearly 1,600 unique viewers.

The international conference “Money & Banking”, which the NBU has organized for the third consecutive year, has become a great tradition. The organizers are inviting scholars to new discussions next year to continue exploring the past and future of money together.

item.title: Oversight Council Conducts Regular Review of Money Market and FX Market Indicators
item.description:
On 31 August 2026, the Oversight Council for Ukrainian Money Market and FX Market Indicators (hereinafter referred to as the “Oversight Council”) conducted the sixth periodic review of the UONIA money market indicator and FX market indicators (the hryvnia’s official exchange rate against foreign currencies, accounting prices for investment metals, and the hryvnia’s reference exchange rate against the U.S. dollar).

This biannual review is aimed at determining whether or not there have been any structural changes in the market and/or other grounds that may indicate the need to replace the existing indicators, adjust their methodology, or address other important aspects of their calculation and publication.

Here are the key conclusions based on the review findings.

  • UONIA money market indicator

Although the current methodology for calculating the UONIA is not perfect, the UONIA remains an objective indicator of the money market That said, there is a need to find ways to improve the UONIA calculation methodology, which is being carried out by the NBU together with a SECO international technical assistance expert.

  • FX market indicators

The official/reference exchange rates of the hryvnia to the U.S. dollar and the methodology for calculating these exchange rates currently meet the market’s conditions and needs. Trading volumes on the FX market are fully sufficient for calculating reliable exchange rate indicators for the hryvnia against the U.S. dollar. Currently, the methodology or other procedures for estimating and releasing the indicators of the UAH/USD foreign-exchange market do not require any changes.

The upward trend in trading volumes in Ukraine’s FX market has persisted over recent years, reflecting a gradual increase in economic activity. The trading volumes in the interbank FX market are rising in both the UAH/USD segment and (to a lesser extent) the UAH/EUR segment. A steady, albeit slow, upward trend in the share of UAH/EUR transactions persists primarily in household deposits and, to a certain extent, in cash transactions.

The implementation of previously approved proposals is ongoing. These include the introduction of a new FX market benchmark – the reference UAH/EUR exchange rate as of 12 p.m. – and revisions to the methodology for calculating official exchange rates for currencies other than the U.S. dollar.

Information messages about the results of the regular review of money market and FX market indicators (MFXMIs) are available at the following links:

  • UONIA money market indicator
  • FX market indicators.
For reference

The Oversight Council was established on 18 August 2023. This collegial body includes NBU employees and external members recommended by the Money Market and FX Market Contact Group.

The Oversight Council is tasked with working out and discussing issues related to the definition, calculation, and publication of MFXMIs. These include: 

  • assessment of the representation performance of MFXMIs
  • development and adjustment of methodology for MFXMIs
  • oversight of the internal control system
  • error-handling policy
  • review of audit results
  • prevention of conflicts of interest
  • consideration of claims
  • data quality control supervision 
  • The compliance of MFXMIs with IOSCO principles. 

The Oversight Council is an advisory body. Any and all decisions regarding MFXMIs are made by the NBU Board.

item.title: NBU Unveils FX Global Code Web Page
item.description:
With the aim of promoting globally recognized principles of the FX market operation, the National Bank of Ukraine is launching a new FX Global Code web page in the FX Market section of its official website.

The new page contains information about the FX Global Code (or the Code),  its core principles, the benefits of adherence, and practical recommendations for Ukrainian FX market participants.

Specifically, the new section includes:

  • general information about the FX Global Code, its purpose, and the basic principles of compliance
  • the Code’s core principles organized around six categories: ethics, governance, execution, information sharing, risk management and compliance, and confirmation and settlement processes
  • the benefits of adhering to the Code for Ukrainian FX market participants
  • guidelines on preparing to adhere to the Code and relevant informational materials
  • the NBU’s Statement of Commitment to the FX Global Code
  • terms of adherence and the list of Ukrainian banks that have adopted the FX Global Code.
For reference:

The FX Global Code sets forth a common set of guidelines to promote the integrity and effective functioning of the global FX market. The Code supplements local laws and regulations by identifying global good practices and processes, and the responsibility for ensuring compliance with its principles rests with the participants themselves.

The Statement of Commitment to the FX Global Code has been published by more than 1,500 FX market participants from various countries, including 56 central banks from Europe and around the world, the European Central Bank, and the Bank for International Settlements.

On 22 May 2026, the NBU adopted the FX Global Code to uphold the highest professional standards in financial markets. The issue of adopting the Code was considered at the meeting of the Money and Foreign Exchange Markets Contact Group. At the meeting, the NBU encouraged banks to consider adhering to the Code, as it will strengthen their reputational capital, increase the confidence of clients and counterparties, expand opportunities for cooperation, and serve as an impetus for improving internal processes.

item.title: NBU September 2026 Inflation Update
item.description:
In September 2026, inflation accelerated to 10.0% yoy. In monthly terms, prices rose 2.1%, according to data published by the State Statistics Service of Ukraine.

Headline inflation significantly exceeded the NBU’s forecast path published in the July 2026 Inflation Report, primarily due to escalated russian attacks on production, storage, and logistics infrastructure, as well as rising fuel prices. Core inflation also came in above the forecast, driven by faster-than-expected increases in the prices of non-food products and processed foods.

Fuel inflation surged to 46.2% yoy

This upswing was driven by sharp fluctuations in global petroleum product prices, whose effects gradually fed through to wholesale and retail prices. Gasoline and diesel prices rose the most, while LPG prices increased considerably more slowly.

Growth in raw food prices picked up tangibly (to 6.7% yoy)

Prices of vegetables in the borshch basket rose faster amid smaller harvests and declining inventories. Egg prices resumed rising after three months of declines, primarily due to higher poultry rearing costs. Price pressures on these goods also intensified because of higher transportation and storage costs.

Cucumber prices increased due to the seasonal decline in the supply of open-field produce and a temporary shortage of greenhouse produce. The decline in apple prices slowed mainly due to a low-base effect from the previous year, while the price decrease for some other fruits decelerated due to a seasonal downturn in supply. Meat prices also declined more slowly: pork prices were supported by higher purchase prices amid a smaller pig herd, stronger demand from processors, and higher feed and energy prices; chicken prices were underpinned by an overall increase in meat product prices and production costs.

Core inflation also increased significantly (to 8.8% yoy)

Price growth for processed food products accelerated (to 10.7% yoy). Non-alcoholic beverages made the largest contribution to this uptrend, reflecting supply shortages caused by damage to production facilities, as well as higher fuel and raw-material costs. Sausages also became noticeably more expensive, as prices for meat raw materials declined more slowly and logistics costs increased. Cheese prices continued to rise due to higher production costs, while fish and seafood prices kept rising because of logistical difficulties and higher energy costs, as well as elevated prices for imported products.

Price growth for non-food products accelerated markedly (to 2.4% yoy), partly due to the effects of russian strikes against the warehousing and logistics infrastructure of retail and pharmaceutical companies.

Services also continued to become more expensive (up 13.7% yoy). Higher-education services made the largest contribution to this increase, particularly as a result of higher faculty salaries. Housing rents also continued to rise amid increased internal migration.

Growth in administered prices accelerated to 13.6% yoy

This uptrend was driven by further increases in public transportation fares, water supply tariffs, and alcoholic beverage prices. Meanwhile, the year-on-year rate of increase in tobacco product prices remained unchanged.

Over the past month, price pressures intensified due to the consequences of russia’s war of aggression and the war in the Middle East. Higher costs of transporting and storing goods, driven by high fuel prices and the destruction of warehousing and logistics infrastructure, will continue to fuel inflationary pressures in the coming months.

These and other factors will inform the revised macroeconomic forecast, which will be released on 29 October 2026, during a press briefing following the monetary policy decision of the NBU Board. The detailed macroeconomic forecast will be published in the Inflation Report on 5 November 2026.

item.title: NBU and International Finance Corporation Continue Cooperation to Develop Digital Financial Services in Ukraine
item.description:
The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, have signed a Cooperation Agreement under the Digital Finance Future Ukraine project (hereinafter referred to as the "Agreement") implemented in partnership with the Swiss State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO).

The Agreement was signed on 12 October 2026, during a meeting between Andriy Pyshnyy, Governor of the NBU, and Alfonso Garcia Mora, IFC Vice President for Europe, Latin America, and the Caribbean, on the sidelines of the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group in Bangkok.

The Agreement aims to develop a modern, secure, and efficient financial sector in Ukraine by expanding cashless and digital financial services, encouraging their use, and improving access to financial products.

The Agreement provides for cooperation between the NBU and IFC in the following areas:

  • financial innovation – supporting the NBU in improving the operation of its regulatory sandbox and open banking framework, establishing an Innovation Hub, and analyzing regulatory and market challenges to strengthen financial inclusion
  • payments and digital resilience – further adopting international best practices for developing cashless payments, particularly instant payments, including mechanisms to encourage their use, as well as supporting efforts to strengthen digital resilience of financial institutions
  • financial literacy and institutional capacity – supporting educational and awareness-raising initiatives related to digital financial services, among other activities.

Implementation of the Digital Finance Future Ukraine project will run until 2029. It follows on from the Digital Financial Services Development project, which ended on 31 December 2024.

"Signing the Agreement is a logical continuation of the substantive work carried out jointly by the NBU and IFC. We particularly appreciate the fact that there was no break between the previous and new phases of cooperation. Throughout 2025–2026, IFC continued to provide expert support to the NBU, which is an important indicator of our partnership. The areas covered by the Agreement are of strategic importance to the NBU, as they concern the development of a modern, competitive, and resilient financial sector aligned with Ukraine’s European aspirations. The NBU is grateful to the IFC team for its consistent support. I expect this Agreement to help us apply international expertise and experience even more quickly to practical solutions for Ukraine’s financial market," said NBU Governor Andriy Pyshnyy.

Background

Since February 2022, IFC, a member of the World Bank Group, has committed over US$3.2 billion in Ukraine, including more than US$1.2 billion mobilized from partners. This support is part of the World Bank Group’s broader response, through which more than US$91 billion has been mobilized for Ukraine.

item.title: NBU Publishes Interim Stocktaking Report on Measures to Liberalize FX Market
item.description:
The National Bank of Ukraine has published the interim report Stocktaking of Measures to Liberalize the FX Market (public version).  The document contains a comprehensive analysis of the already implemented measures to ease FX restrictions and outlines the prospects for FX liberalization.

Easing of FX Restrictions: Principles, Stages, and Prerequisites

The NBU has been systematically implementing FX liberalization measures in line with the Strategy for Easing FX Restrictions, Transitioning to Greater Flexibility of the Exchange Rate, and Returning to Inflation Targeting (hereinafter referred to as the “Strategy”), adopted in July 2023. The ultimate goal is to return FX regulation to its level before the full-scale war.

The general logic and sequence of FX liberalization steps are set out in the Roadmap for Gradual Easing of FX Restrictions (hereinafter referred to as the “Roadmap”). To date, the majority of stage-one steps have been completed, significant progress has been made in introducing stage-two measures, and the implementation of certain stage-three measures has begun.

Decisions to implement FX liberalization measures are based on a comprehensive assessment of the overall macroeconomic, market, and financial conditions, including:

  • the inflation rate and inflation expectations
  • the level of international reserves and FX market sustainability
  • interest rates and the attractiveness of hryvnia instruments
  • financial stability parameters.

In addition, the NBU is engaged in an ongoing dialogue with stakeholders (the government, international organizations, business associations, the expert community) to identify the most pressing needs for easing FX restrictions. The results of these consultations are taken into account when structuring the next packages of FX liberalization measures.

This balanced approach has made it possible to expand opportunities for businesses and households without creating significant additional demand for foreign currency, pressure on international reserves, or risks to price and financial stability.

Progress in Implementing the Roadmap and Achievements of FX Liberalization

The active phase of FX liberalization began in May 2024, when the NBU adopted the first major package of measures to ease the FX restrictions. Overall, 154 measures have been implemented under the Roadmap, including 144 measures to ease FX restrictions and 10 measures to prevent the circumvention of the existing restrictions.

The implementation of measures under the Roadmap has made it possible to significantly improve the business and financial sector environment, and has also enabled the population not only to meet their basic needs but also, to some extent, to diversify their savings and develop an investment culture.

Current transactions have mostly been liberalized for legal persons. Economic incentives have also been put in place to attract new investments and loans. Foreign investors are free to invest in the capital of Ukrainian enterprises, provide loans, repatriate profits, and receive timely repayments of interest and principal.

Stimulating liberalization is gaining traction. Its broad range of measures includes incentives to attract new capital. Businesses are able to make important transactions beyond existing restrictions, as long as this is done without exceeding the investment limit, the donation limit, the loan limit, and the additional limit. A total of USD 1,504 million in transactions has been made under stimulating liberalization, and up to USD 875 million can still be transferred abroad before current limits are maxed out.

Individuals are allowed to purchase cash foreign currency without restrictions. It has also been permitted, within established limits, to purchase cashless foreign currency, investment metals, and securities of foreign issuers, as well as to make card payments on foreign websites. Non-residents are now allowed to purchase and transfer foreign currency within the limits of funds received as wages or equivalent payments. Ukrainians abroad are able pay, within the established limits, for goods and services and housing rental from hryvnia accounts using both cards and the SWIFT system. Payments for goods and services from FX cards can be made without a limit, while payments for jewelry and housing rental are permitted subject to a limit.

Banks have been permitted, when calculating their FX position, to gradually include the portion of loan loss provisions that was previously excluded from the calculation.

Insurers have been authorized to make payments in foreign currency for reinsurance with non-residents, both directly and through reinsurance brokers. Furthermore, under insurance contracts, it is now possible to make insurance payments and refund insurance premiums in foreign currency to non-residents. 

Assessment of the Effectiveness of the Measures Taken in Terms of Their Impact on the Economy and the FX Market

Measures to ease FX restrictions were structured and prioritized in such a way as to contribute to bringing the economy out of the shadow and creating conditions for the recovery of economic growth.

The NBU has structured each liberalization measure in such a way as to eliminate the possibilities to circumvent FX restrictions and prevent unproductive capital outflows. As a result, the share of FX purchases and cross-border transfers related to the liberalization has consistently been around 4% and 6% of total FX purchases and transfers, respectively. At the same time, about 30% of transfers by volume is made using companies’ own foreign exchange.

Further Prospects for FX Liberalization

Easing the FX market controls remains a priority for the NBU. FX liberalization should continue to be comprehensive, meaning that it should cover as many different areas and categories as possible: businesses, households, and the financial sector. 

Subsequent steps will be implemented gradually and will be conditioned on the availability of appropriate macroeconomic prerequisites and will take into account designated priorities, including efforts to attract investment to the Ukrainian economy. Each measure will continue to be accompanied by strict monitoring and control mechanisms to prevent the circumvention of the FX restrictions that remain in place.

Overall, FX liberalization measures will continue to be considered in the context of the comprehensive application of monetary policy instruments and exchange rate policy, as envisaged by the Strategy.

For reference

A comprehensive analysis of measures to ease FX restrictions has been conducted in line with the commitments under paragraph 49 of the Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies with the International Monetary Fund (IMF). The IMF confirmed the successful fulfillment of the relevant commitment.

The quantitative analysis of the effects of FX liberalization is based on information and data available as of 15 August 2026.

item.title: International Reserves at USD 47.1 billion as of End-September
item.description:
According to preliminary data, Ukraine had USD 47,101.8 million in international reserves as of 1 October 2026. In September, the reserves decreased by 3.2%. These dynamics were driven by the NBU’s FX interventions and Ukraine’s FX debt repayments. These transactions exceeded inflows from international partners and proceeds from conversion into the hryvnia of foreign currency funds received under the Ukraine Support Loan. International reserves are currently sufficient for maintaining the FX market sustainability.

In general, several factors determined the dynamics of international reserves in September 2026.

First, the NBU’s transactions in the Ukrainian FX market

In September, the NBU sold USD 5,449.9 million on the FX market, according to balance sheet data.

Second, inflows to the government’s accounts and the servicing and repayment of public debt

A total of USD 890.4 million came into the government's FX accounts with the NBU through the World Bank’s accounts in September.

In addition, Ukraine received a defense tranche of USD 3.81 billion from the EU under the Ukraine Support Loan. These funds are not included into Ukraine’s international reserves due to restricted (targeted) use of the funds. However, if the government sells these funds to the NBU for the hryvnia for targeted use, the international reserves will increase by this amount. In September, the government converted USD 3.81 billion of these funds into the hryvnia, which respectively increased international reserves. At the same time, it should be considered that hryvnia financing at the expense of these funds leads to a subsequent increase in demand on the FX market affecting volumes of the NBU’s FX interventions. Thus, the NBU’s transactions with these funds actually have a redistributing function.

A total of USD 195.7 million was spent on servicing and repaying the FX public debt, including:

  • USD 72.3 million to service and repay the debt to the World Bank
  • USD 8.3 million to service FX domestic government debt securities
  • USD 115.1 million to meet the country’s liabilities to other creditors.

In addition, Ukraine repaid USD 254.3 million to the International Monetary Fund.

Third, the revaluation of financial instruments (due to changes in their market value and exchange rate fluctuations), and the impact of other factors.

In September, due to revaluation of financial instruments and the impact of other factors, international reserves decreased in value by USD 368.3 million.

International reserves are now covering 4.0 months of future imports.

Data on international reserves and FX liquidity are compiled and released on a monthly basis:  

  • for preliminary data, no later than on the 7th day after the reporting month ends
  • for revised data, no later than on the 21st day after the reporting month ends.

Revised data are available here.

item.title: NBU Discloses Main Principle for Determining Volumes of Three-Month Certificates of Deposit Placements
item.description:
The National Bank of Ukraine is informing market participants of the main principle for determining the volumes of three-month certificates of deposit (CDs) placements through interest rate tenders. The purpose of this measure is to maintain competition among banks for depositors and to ensure that hryvnia savings remain attractive.

When determining the volumes of three-month CDs placements, the NBU takes into account the aggregate limit on banks’ purchases of such CDs. Changes in the aggregate limit affect placement volumes. This approach makes it possible to maintain a link between banks’ acceptance of hryvnia term deposits from the households and their ability to invest funds in three-month CDs, and increases price competition among banks in interest rate tenders.

Going forward, the NBU plans to increase the transparency of the parameters for placing three-month CDs as the operational framework of its interest rate policy evolves.

A proposal to disclose the principle of determining the volume of three-month CD placements was put forward at a meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee on 16 September 2026.

For reference

On 30 July 2026, the NBU announced the launch of the modernization of the operational framework for its interest rate policy. The strategic objective of this modernization is to stimulate the money market and foster the development of reliable market benchmarks for pricing.  Ultimately, the changes will strengthen the NBU’s ability to fulfil the primary objective of monetary policy – maintaining price stability – by enhancing the effectiveness of monetary transmission.

As part of the first stage of the transformation, which took effect on 7 August 2026, changes were made to the mechanism for conducting transactions involving three-month limited CDs.

The NBU will implement the subsequent steps gradually and will communicate them following the adoption of the relevant decisions.  They will continue to take into account the need to maintain appropriately tight monetary conditions to ensure price stability, while also preserving incentives for banks to compete for depositors

item.title: Businesses Report Cautious Economic Outlook – Business Outlook Survey in September
item.description:
Businesses reported guarded expectations for their economic performance in September. The further deterioration of the security situation, the destruction of logistics, production and warehouse facilities, rising business costs driven by higher fuel prices, the limited domestic supply of goods and services, a shortage of skilled labor, and a slight worsening of exchange rate expectations constrained businesses’ economic activity. Positive factors included a stable energy sector, a bumper harvest, and new logistics routes. This is evidenced by the business activity expectations index (BAEI), which the NBU calculates every month, apart from a forced break in March–May 2022. The BAEI was 48.2 in September 2026, compared to 48.3 in August 2026 and 50.4 in September 2025.

Industrial companies returned to reporting a positive economic outlook, thanks to the improved performance of the manufacturing industry and a stable energy sector, the sectoral index being 51.0 in September, compared to 47.3 in August and 49.1 in September 2025. In contrast to the previous month, respondents expected a rise in the amount of manufactured goods and in the number of new orders for products, including export orders. Respondents also expected an increase in their stocks of raw materials and supplies. In contrast, respondents remained downbeat about the amount of unfinished products (unfulfilled orders) and finished goods stocks.

In view of the suspension of state funding for road and infrastructure restoration, the seasonal nature of construction work, and rising costs, construction companies reported a cautious economic outlook following six months of optimism, the sectoral index being 48.8 in September, compared to 50.7 in August and 50.0 in September 2025. Companies continued to expect an increase in their construction volumes, the number of new orders, and in purchases of raw materials and supplies, albeit at a slower pace. Respondents said they intended to purchase fewer contractor services on the back of persistent growth in the cost of these services. At the same time, respondents softened their still guarded expectations about the availability of contractors.

Trading companies had the most restrained expectations among all sectors regarding their current economic performance, given the ongoing destruction of warehouse facilities along with high-cost and complex logistics, the sectoral index being 45.9 in September, compared to 47.5 in August and 54.0 in September 2025. Respondents expected a further decrease in their trade turnovers, the amount of goods purchased for sale, and in their stocks of goods for sale. Respondents declared intentions to cut their trade margins further.

Due to the ongoing destruction of logistics and warehouse facilities, higher fuel prices, and a shortage of skilled labor, services companies reported more restrained expectations for their current performance, the sectoral index being 47.3 in September, compared to 49.5 in August and 49.4 in September 2025. Companies expected the amount of services provided to be unchanged on the previous month. In contrast to the previous month, respondents expected a decrease in the number of new orders for services and in the amount of services that are being provided.

Most respondents across all of the surveyed sectors expected more rapid growth in purchase prices / raw material and supplies prices, declaring intentions to raise their selling prices at a faster pace.

The labor market situation remained challenging. Only construction companies continued to report intentions to expand their workforces, while companies in other sectors said they intended to lay off staff, with the strongest intentions expressed by services companies.

Background

This survey was carried out from 3 September through 22 September 2026. A total of 588 companies were polled. Of the companies polled, 43.0% are industrial companies, 25.9% services companies, 24.7% trading companies, and 6.5% construction companies; 31.6% of the respondents are large companies, 29.1% medium companies, and 39.3% small companies. Of the surveyed companies, 34.5% are both exporters and importers, 8.2% are exporters only, 18.5% are importers only, and 38.8% are neither exporters nor importers.

The findings presented reflect only the opinions of the respondents (top managers of companies), and should not be considered as NBU assessments.

The monthly business activity expectations index (BAEI) is a tool for conducting the latest assessments and detecting trends in economic development. It is calculated on the basis of surveys of Ukrainian real sector companies regarding changes in their performance compared to the previous month.

Monthly business activity expectations indices are calculated on the basis of respondents’ replies. These indices are as follows: sectoral indices (for each sector of the economy) and a composite index (describes the country’s economic performance over a month). A value of 50 corresponds to the neutral level. Index values above the neutral level indicate positive expectations.

Read more about the September 2026 survey in the Monthly Surveys of Companies Subsection of the Publications Section on the NBU’s official website.

The NBU posts monthly survey results in the open data format.

The results of the next survey (for October 2026) will be published on the first business day of November 2026.

item.title: Outcomes of the 10th Annual Research Conference of the Central Banks of Ukraine and Poland
item.description:
The 10th Annual Research Conference on Central Banks’ Response to Future Challenges: Resilience, Credibility, and Innovation was held online on 21–22 September 2026, bringing together 60 speakers from more than 20 countries. Participants included central bank governors, policymakers from international financial institutions, and researchers from leading universities around the world. The event featured a rich program of opening remarks, two keynote addresses, five panel discussions, 12 research presentations, and three special video addresses.

Opening the conference, National Bank of Ukraine Governor Andriy Pyshnyy posed a fundamental question for the agenda: "What should central banks be like in a world where change happens faster than we can get used to the last round of changes?"

“The answer to the challenges of the future is not to learn how to predict every shock that may come next. It is to build and preserve institutions capable of performing their function even when forecasts become obsolete, traditional instruments stop working, and there is no tested recipe to follow,” Andriy Pyshnyy said.

In his welcome address to conference participants, the NBU Governor proposed three key prompts for discussion:

  • resilience is impossible without flexibility, but flexibility needs an anchor
  • credibility requires openness, and openness requires accountability
  • innovation expands our capabilities, but it does not relieve us of responsibility.

An important part of the discussions was the NBU’s unique experience of operating under extreme conditions, an experience that continues to evolve as russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine continues.

Keynote addresses were delivered by Oesterreichische Nationalbank Governor Martin Kocher and 2024 Nobel Prize laureate in economic sciences Simon Johnson

Martin Kocher spoke about independence, credibility, and the ability of monetary policy to respond to shocks. He noted that a credible central bank is not one that always does the same thing, but one whose different actions are understood by the public and markets as serving a single objective: maintaining price stability. At the same time, he stressed that flexibility cannot work without an anchor. A well-functioning economic policy regime should rest on at least four elements: first, a common objective across policy branches; second, durability; third, expertise, including openness to new evidence; and fourth, traceability and transparency.

Simon Johnson’s keynote focused on the implications and opportunities arising from rapid technological development. He explained how artificial intelligence (AI) could reshape the economic and political realities of many countries and why it should be directed toward expanding the number of tasks that require human involvement, rather than deepening labor market polarization and inequality. He also noted that Ukraine is an example of a country with deep technological expertise and impressive innovation, including in the use of AI.

Special addresses were delivered by Bank of Italy Governor Fabio Panetta, International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, and European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde

Fabio Panetta placed particular emphasis on the credibility of central banks. One of his key conclusions was that credibility is not something that can be built during a crisis. He stressed that credibility is developed over years through strong institutions, consistent policies, and a willingness to undertake difficult reforms. Today, this also requires central banks to adapt to rapid technological change while remaining focused on fulfilling their mandates. Fabio Panetta also highlighted the NBU’s experience: despite exceptionally difficult conditions, it has succeeded in maintaining monetary and financial stability while adapting its instruments to wartime needs.

Kristalina Georgieva presented four lessons on resilience drawn from the NBU’s experience that are relevant to other central banks and the international financial community:

  • resilience must be built well before it is tested. Banking sector reforms, stronger supervision, the accumulation of reserves, the development of digital financial infrastructure, and the strengthening of the NBU’s independence laid the foundation for the financial system’s resilience after russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine
  • resilience requires the ability to adapt. Emergency measures taken in the first days of the full-scale invasion helped prevent panic and preserve stability, after which the NBU adapted its policies and began their gradual normalization
  • in conditions of extreme uncertainty, human capital is critical. Data, research, professional expertise, scenario analysis, and planning for different possible developments became the basis for the NBU’s decisions and an important component of Ukraine’s programs with the IMF
  • resilience depends on credibility. Credibility of the NBU and Ukraine’s other economic institutions matters to citizens and businesses and, during the war, is also important for maintaining large-scale international financial support.

Christine Lagarde commended the NBU’s work during the full-scale invasion, including keeping the financial system and payments functioning without interruption, strengthening banks’ resilience, gradually normalizing monetary policy, and taking decisions aimed at reinforcing credibility. She also placed particular emphasis on support for Ukraine from its European partners and on cooperation between the ECB and the NBU.

“The people of Ukraine know the storm, and after years of war, they continue to defend their freedom and show the world the meaning of strength. But we can also see that strength in the institutions that continue to serve the Ukrainian people. Ukraine will weather this storm, too,” Christine Lagarde concluded.

The conference provided a platform for exchanging experience on policymaking amid large-scale shocks

The approaches developed through the event will help central banks preserve resilience and credibility and effectively implement innovation as they respond to future challenges.

“Conference participants emphasized that in an era of constant shocks, central banks must be flexible and adaptable; however, this flexibility is effective only when underpinned by a strong anchor – an unwavering commitment to price stability and institutional independence,” NBU Deputy Governor Volodymyr Lepushynskyi said in summing up the event.

The 10th Annual Research Conference was organized by the National Bank of Ukraine jointly with Narodowy Bank Polski, with the support of partners including the International Monetary Fund and the STEP IN 2 EU international cooperation program. We sincerely thank the participants and partners for their support in making this important research event possible.
